title: Resume Formatting: What Recruiters Look at First (6-Second Resume Scan)
description:
Recruiters decide whether to read a resume in seconds — and most qualified candidates get skipped because the top section of their resume doesn’t clearly show value.

In this video, I break down what recruiters look at first on a resume and how to format the top quarter of your resume so you make it past the 6-second resume scan. You’ll learn how recruiters actually scan resumes, what information they look for immediately, and how to position yourself as the person who can solve the role’s core problem.

This video is Part 1 of my Get Seen series, where I help job seekers turn resumes and job search materials into interview requests — and this is the perfect place to start.

In this video, you’ll learn:

• What belongs in the top section of a resume
• How recruiters scan resumes in the first 6 seconds
• How to position your resume headline and summary for impact
• How to show you’re the solution to the role — fast

 Free cheat sheet linked in the comments to help you apply this quickly

transcript: Recruiters do not read résumés. They scan them and in about six seconds they decide whether yours is worth a deeper look or whether it disappears into the void where résumés go to die. And yes, we are going to raise yours from the dead today. If your resume isn't getting traction, it's usually not because you aren't qualified. It's because your value isn't clear fast enough. In this video, I'm going to show you exactly what belongs in the top corner of your resume so a recruiter immediately understands why you're relevant and why they should keep reading and invite you in for that interview. And at the end, I've linked a free cheat sheet to help you apply this without overthinking it. If we haven't met yet, I'm Kate Kersner, a career strategist with 20 years of experience helping qualified people stop getting overlooked. Just think of me as your new career bestie. This is my first video in the get seen series because one of the most gut-wrenching parts of job searching is feeling invisible, even when you know you're really good at what you do. So, let's fix that. Here's what most people don't realize. Recruiters decide whether to keep reading based almost entirely on the top quarter of your resume, which includes your headline and your professional summary. Most job seekers build resumes by listing experienced strong candidates do something different. They position themselves as a solution. Let me show you what I mean. When I work with a job description, I ask one simple question. What problem is this role designed to solve? I did this recently for a VP of HR role. The posting mentioned a merger growth and multi-sight complexity. When we asked that question, the answer was clear. This role exists to lead people strategy through organizational change and build HR systems that can scale. [music] Once you know that, designing the top of your resume stops feeling overwhelming. Let's start with the resume headline. Your headline should be the job title you're applying to, plus three core skills pulled directly from the job description. Not personality traits, not buzzwords, and not every responsibility you've ever [music] had. Just list the skills needed to solve the problem. The problem wasn't run HR. It was leading change across growing [music] multi-sight organizations and building people systems that held up under pressure. So instead of listing everything, [music] we chose three skills that immediately signal I've done this before. [music] Here's what that looked like as a headline. VP of human resources, organizational change and integration, [music] executive partnership and people strategy, scalable HR systems and compliance. Each part maps directly back to the problem. Organizational change and integration tells them you've led through complexity. Executive partnership and people strategy tells them you operate at the leadership level. Scalable HR systems and compliance tells them you build systems that work at scale even when stuff hits the fan. In six seconds, the recruiter knows what level you operate at, what challenges you've handled, and why you're relevant. And that's the goal. Now, let's talk about the professional summary because this is where most résumés fall apart. The biggest mistake I see is treating the summary like a mini biography. People list years of experience, responsibilities, and what I hate most, buzzwords, and they never connect it back to why the role exists. Instead of asking, "What have I done?" you ask, "How have I solved this kind of problem before?" Here's an example of a professional summary written from that lens. Senior HR leader with 15 years of experience guiding organizations through growth, integration, and multi-sight operational complexity. Led acquisition and workforce transitions, impacting 4,000 employees, delivering a 50% year-over-year turnover reduction and improving employment eligibility compliance from 70 to 95%. Trusted executive partner known for turning change into consistent employee experiences. audit ready HR systems and leaders who perform at scale. If a recruiter stopped reading right there, they already know three things. This person operates at the right level. They understand the problem and they've solved it before. And that is the entire point. Your professional summary isn't there to tell your life story. It's there to convince someone that you belong in the conversation and you are worth the interview. When your headline [music] signals the problem you solve and your summary proves it, [music] you stop getting it skimmed and start getting seen and you have won the six-second scan. I linked a free cheat sheet in the comments to help you apply this right away. And if you want help building résumés and job search strategies, I've also linked my get seen resume and job search [music] strategy guide. Make sure you're subscribed because in the next videos I give you the [music] system to construct a professional summary like the one we just walked through step by [music] step. You are not invisible. You just need a better strategy to be seen. And that is exactly what your career bestie is here to help you
